articles.title_zh: Defiant Hegseth tells Democrats their impeachment push ‘won’t work’
articles.content_orig:
US Secretary of Defence also vows to press ahead with Trump’s agenda, urges Congress to approve at least US$350 billion in defence funding
US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth said he will “not back down” against a “lame duck” Congress, and that the drives for his impeachment will “not work” in his first reaction after Democrats’ landslide victory in Tuesday’s election.
In a video uploaded by the Pentagon on Thursday, Hegseth said that “a disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies,” have been submitting bills for his impeachment, resembling that of the similar attempt against US President Donald Trump.
Hegseth was referring to Thomas Massie, a Republican House representative from Kentucky who has called for a vote to impeach Hegseth as soon as the Congress session resumes after the midterm election. Earlier this year, he was ruled out of the House race after a Trump-backed candidate was instead nominated to run for his seat.

articles.title_orig: France strikes: largest day of protests in years as economy fuels unrest
articles.title_zh: France strikes: largest day of protests in years as economy fuels unrest
articles.content_orig:
The head of France's CGT labour union, Sophie Binet (C), said the wave of protests and strikes had reached a new level
More than 600,000 protesters have taken part in rallies and marches across France, according to France's interior ministry, with five unions joining a day of action demanding more money for wages and public services.
The left-wing CGT union put the number of people taking part in Thursday's mobilisation at 1.57 million and hailed the figure as "a level unmatched" since 2023, citing big protests in Paris, Marseille, Bordeaux and Lille.
As darkness fell in Paris, Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu said he would convene a "social conference" with unions and employers next Monday.
The wave of protests began in September over poor conditions and resources at lycÃ©es (high schools), before spreading to universities, workers and a revived "yellow-vest" movement against high prices.
The unions had vowed to take the co-ordinated move against the government "to the next level", and CGT chief Sophie Binet had said their message was that "the only thing that will bring this mobilisation to a halt is responding to our demands".
Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez had earlier deployed 70,000 police, vowing "an extremely firm response" to any potential outbreaks of violence.
Some unrest was reported in several cities.
A car was set alight near the Gallieni bridge over the RhÃ´ne river in Lyon, as hundreds of activists from the radical left-wing "black bloc" clashed with police.
Clashes were also reported in the north-western city of Rennes, where the local prefect said a "hostile group of masked individuals" had gathered in front of the main union march. Tear gas was used to clear a square in the south-western city of Bordeaux and a teenager was hurt in a stabbing involving a student at a high-school blockade in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris.
But the trouble was not on the scale seen during the last big day of protests, on Saturday 17 October, when more than 2,000 stores were looted and historic buildings set on fire.
The provisional numbers reported on Thursday were higher than on 17 October, considered  the biggest day of rallies until now when the interior ministry said 550,000 people had turned out and the unions counted 800,000.
Earlier on Thursday the leader of the CFDT union, Marylise LÃ©on, said she would be happy if the protests matched that earlier level.
A car was set alight during a protest in the centre of Lyon
A coalition of unions across the public and private sector had urged workers, pensioners and young people to join Thursday's day of strikes to intensify pressure on the government. In particular they are seeking a rise in the minimum wage, or Smic , which is currently â¬12.31 (Â£10) an hour.
Sophie Binet told reporters at the start of a march in central Paris that protesters had "just reached a new level in their mobilisation" and were demanding immediate answers.
An estimated 9.89% of civil servants were taking part in the strikes, according to government figures.
Disruption was reported in schools, hospitals and public transport, and the Eiffel Tower and some exhibition rooms at the Louvre museum in Paris had to close.
Workers were also asked to halt production at oil refineries and France was expected to import more electricity than it produced on Thursday because of disruption at nuclear plants.
Disruption was already reported at schools on Thursday morning
The head of the CFDT complained that it was not just the minimum wage that needed to increase. "We are asking for a net increase of â¬100 a month," Marylise LÃ©on explained.
The government has sought to appease public anger over rising prices, bringing down the cost of fuel by releasing 10 million barrels of diesel from strategic reserves. Ministers have also promised school students to reform the unpopular Parcoursup university admissions platform and eventually replace it by 2028.
The prime minister said early on Thursday evening that Monday's "social conference" with unions and employers would seek to "provide answers to questions surrounding purchasing power and wages".
However, the government by its own admission has little room to manoeuvre, as it looks to make tens of billions of euros in savings, in a bid to cut the budget deficit to 5% of GDP.
The education ministry said that 16% of teachers had gone on strike on Thursday, and the unions said disruption had affected more than one in four lycÃ©es, which cater for 15-18 year-olds, as well as the vast majority of universities.
"Now it's not only about [investing in] public services in education and higher education, it's about all of the public services in France," the vice-president of the Unef student union, Alice De Brito, told the BBC.
Meanwhile, a revived gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement that staged a revolt against the high cost of living several years ago has called for further blockades and protests on Friday and Saturday too.
'Everyone hates the police' â what France's school protests reveal about a divided nation
France launches attempted murder investigation after petrol bomb thrown at police
Thursday's march was eventually allowed in central Paris, although not along the route proposed by the unions between Place de la Bastille and Place de la Concorde, which would have taken protesters near the National Assembly, the ÃlysÃ©e Palace, and the prime minister's residence at HÃ´tel Matignon.
Instead, the march followed another central route from Place de la RÃ©publique to Place de la Nation.
The interior minister had earlier spoken of three potential risks on Thursday, from radical left "black blocs" groups and looting to wildcat marches without union authorisation.

articles.title_orig: Dow drops 1,800 points; Nasdaq tumbles into correction territory on AI tech wreck: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow drops 1,800 points; Nasdaq tumbles into correction territory on AI tech wreck: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
The Nasdaq Composite plunged into correction territory on Thursday. History shows more selling can follow in the near term, but a recovery eventually takes hold three months later.
The tech-heavy index slid more than 5% on Thursday, closing more than 11% below its record reached last month. On Wall Street, any decline greater than 10% is a correction. A 20% pullback qualifies as a bear market.
Across 10 previous correction episodes over the last decade, selloffs in 2025, 2022, 2020 and 2018 were followed by further rough selling over the next one month. But the Nasdaq was back to rally mode again after six months for all those occasions except one: 2022.
Overall, the Nasdaq gained an average of 9.41% from the correction bottom over the following three months and 17.03% over six months.
The January 2022 correction was the one that offered a harsher outcome. The Nasdaq lost another 18.3% over the next six months and was down 24.3% a year later.
The catalyst for this correction was Democrats sweeping the House and Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections. The party also made significant gains in Texas, where Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor after campaigning on an immediate moratorium for data center development.
Investors are now weighing whether tighter state-level restrictions could slow data center construction, putting pressure on companies tied to the artificial intelligence trade.
Frank Cappelleri, founder of CappThesis, pointed to past midterm election cycles for guidance and found that points to more volatility in the near term as well.
The chart analyst said the Nasdaq was higher 12 months after the election in all but one of 13 midterm cycles since 1974.
"The caveat is that the path can be a volatile one," he said.
Cappelleri pointed to 2018, when the Nasdaq rallied the day after Democrats won the House. A sharp December sell-off followed, but the index was ultimately about 15% higher a year after the election, he said.
Chip stocks tumbled Thursday, with the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) falling 12% and for its worst day since the Covid-19 breakout of March 2020.
— CNBC's Fred Imbert contributed to the report

articles.title_orig: Tech Billionaires Face Tricky Political Waters After Democratic Midterm Sweep
articles.title_zh: Tech Billionaires Face Tricky Political Waters After Democratic Midterm Sweep
articles.content_orig:
America's billionaires woke up Wednesday to a political reckoning — and a Wall Street rally.
As Democrats celebrated a sweeping midterm victory , some of the country's wealthiest donors traded barbs over record election spending . Others warned the results could threaten the artificial intelligence boom.
Wall Street, however, cheered the outcome. The Dow Jones Industrial Average soared 1,569 points, or 3%, while the S&P 500 gained 1.6% and the Nasdaq Composite rose 1.4%, as investors welcomed political gridlock , reduced uncertainty and President Donald Trump's willingness to accept the results.
Virgin Group founder Richard Branson took aim at the billions spent influencing the election.
"I have felt embarrassed by the billions that tech entrepreneurs and hedge fund managers have spent," Branson wrote Wednesday on LinkedIn , calling for campaign finance reform. Branson did not give donations that met the reporting threshold in the 2026 election cycle.
His comments came as Elon Musk, the election's largest individual donor , watched his preferred Republicans lose the Texas Senate and governor races despite pouring $224 million into the state — nearly half his record $474 million in political giving nationwide, according to a CNBC analysis of campaign finance records.
Early Wednesday, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO suggested on X that data centers in space were looking increasingly appealing before joking that his "election-interfering space lasers" had failed.
LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman , another major political donor, took a sharper tone.
"We should get money out of politics," Hoffman wrote late Tuesday on X , accusing Musk of spending "outrageous amounts to keep authoritarian clowns in power" while defending his own contributions to Democrats.
Other Democratic megadonors celebrated. "The world changed yesterday," Alex Soros wrote Wednesday on X, hailing the results as a generational victory after his family contributed roughly $103 million to Democratic political efforts.
But beyond the political sparring, some of the country's richest investors were focused on a potentially bigger consequence of the Democratic sweep : the future of the AI boom .
Even before polls closed Tuesday, Pershing Square founder Bill Ackman warned on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" that slowing AI development could jeopardize America's technological edge. "Practically speaking, we can't slow down," he said.
As results rolled in Tuesday night, billionaire investor Chamath Palihapitiya sounded an even starker warning.
Palihapitiya initially questioned whether the early results would hold, but warned that if they did, the implications for the AI trade could be severe.
"And the only way to sink the AI trade is to sink the data centers," Palihapitiya said during an election night livestream of the "All-In" podcast.
Texas offered an early test of those fears. Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, who has proposed a moratorium on new data center construction until stronger safeguards are established, defeated three-term Republican incumbent Greg Abbott.
During the same livestream, Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner warned the Democratic wave could mean at least 10 to 15 gigawatts of expected AI data center capacity would not come online in 2027. Wall Street analyst Dan Ives estimated Wednesday that 10% of planned U.S. data centers would no longer go ahead.
Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su acknowledged the growing resistance to AI's expansion , urging technology companies to demonstrate the benefits of data centers to local communities.
"At the end of the day, what we need to do is ensure that everybody wins from AI," Su told CNBC on Wednesday .
Yet Wall Street may have found opportunity in the same slowdown that worried AI's biggest backers.
Fewer new data centers could increase the value of existing facilities while easing the enormous spending burden on technology giants. Big Tech stocks surged Wednesday , adding more than $750 billion in market value at one point, even as smaller, debt-dependent data center operators tumbled.

articles.title_zh: 2 arrested after mushroom gummies given to children on Halloween in Ocean Beach
articles.content_orig:

Two men were taken into custody Wednesday after allegedly distributing psilocybin-infused “magic mushroom” gummies to at least 15 young trick-or-treaters in California’s Ocean Beach on Halloween night .
San Diego Police arrested Michael Goff, 80, and Shawn Michael Foster, 45, following a Wednesday morning search warrant served at a residence on the 2100 block of Sunset Cliffs Boulevard. Both men were booked into the San Diego County Jail on suspicion of being convicted felons in possession of firearms and ammunition.
Although direct charges related to the drug distribution have not yet been filed, officers located a bag of psilocybin gummies inside the residence identical to the packages turned over by parents, as reported by NBC 7 San Diego .
The incident occurred Saturday evening when children between the ages of 1 and 6 retrieved packages from a bowl left on the home’s front porch. Local parents Frank Cary and Cameron Hunter, who were walking a few yards behind their children, noticed the unusual packaging and intervened.
Cary told NBC 7 San Diego that he took one of the bags from his 2-year-old child after noticing a design featuring a giraffe with melting text. Inspecting the label, he found a listed dosage of 5 grams along with text reading “psilocybin mushrooms.”
“So... today I actually found drugs in my kid's Halloween candy,” Hunter wrote in a Facebook post . “5 grams of shroom gummies. Me and another dad confronted the house. 90s were right, I guess.”
Parents confronted a resident at the scene before filing a police report and handing the packages over to police, where later testing confirmed the presence of psilocybin.
When approached at the home on Monday, a resident identifying himself as Shawn Barger disputed the parents’ account, claiming his wife was merely confused when confronted by neighbors on Saturday night.
During the execution of the search warrant, detectives seized an illegally possessed rifle, a partially assembled pistol, dozens of live ammunition rounds, over 2.5 pounds of cannabis, more than 25 grams of crystal methamphetamine, a digital scale, packaging materials and sales ledgers.
A San Diego code compliance investigator also responded to the property to evaluate unpermitted living structures on the site.
The San Diego Police Department's Narcotics Unit and Crime Stoppers are seeking additional information from the public regarding the case.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia's Huang is asked to brief Congress on reported Chinese spy relationship
articles.title_zh: Nvidia's Huang is asked to brief Congress on reported Chinese spy relationship
articles.content_orig:
Three House Republican committee leaders asked Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to sit for a closed-door briefing on his relationship with a tech executive reportedly identified as a Chinese intelligence asset.
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the GOP lawmakers wrote in a letter to Huang unveiled Thursday, using the acronym for the People's Republic of China.
They are seeking information on Huang's interactions with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage," they wrote in the brief message, which is dated Wednesday.
The letter does not specify which reports it is referring to. But The New York Times reported last week that U.S. intelligence found Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen determined to be funneling information to Beijing, had "developed a close relationship" with Jensen Huang.
President Donald Trump , who himself has forged close ties with Jensen Huang as he champions the U.S. artificial intelligence industry, was briefed about a year ago on those intelligence findings, the Times reported.
Trump "chose not to do anything with the information," according to the newspaper, which cited interviews with people briefed on the surveillance and other sources.
The letter to Huang was signed by House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark.
Nvidia did not directly respond when asked by CNBC to comment on the letter and confirm whether Huang would attend the lawmakers' proposed briefing.
It instead provided a statement that largely mirrored the one it previously sent the Times, in which a Nvidia spokesperson suggested Jensen Huang's interactions with Alice Huang were no different than his meetings with other executive clients.
"Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security," the spokesperson said in the statement.
"Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year," the spokesperson said. "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know."
A spokeswoman for Mast did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for additional information. An email to Megaspeed seeking comment was not immediately returned.
The lawmakers invited the Nvidia CEO to appear for an in-person joint briefing on Nov. 18. Nvidia is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17.
"China's access to that sensitive U.S. tech is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress," the committee leaders wrote. "It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk."

articles.content_orig:

It's a big day for Zelda fans. Today (Nov. 5) sees the launch of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake, and retailers could mark the occasion with a restock of the limited-edition Zelda-themed Nintendo Switch 2 console and matching Zelda-themed Pro controller. And I'm tracking stock now.
Anything Zelda-related will sell out fast, and since this console was revealed and pre-orders went live in early September, it's been very tough to find in stock. But Nintendo has promised more is on the way, and Ocarina of Time launch day seems like the perfect time for more restock.
As of now, there is no Zelda Switch 2 restock available . Target, Walmart and Best Buy are all reported to have in-store drops, so check your nearest locations. Meanwhile, Target previously confirmed it will restock the Zelda Switch 2 online on Friday (Nov. 6) . Here's hoping more follow suit.
I've been covering pre-order events and restocks at Tom's Guide for more than five years and have helped thousands of gamers secure limited edition items during that time. Today I'm using all my experience to bring you the latest Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition Switch 2 stock updates.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has been remade for the Nintendo Switch 2. One of the N64's most beloved games has been completely overhauled to celebrate the franchise's 40th Anniversary. The remake offers truly stunning visuals with 4K graphics, overhauled controls, and reworked puzzles.
I'm a Senior Entertainment Editor at Tom's Guide and a more recent convert to The Legend of Zelda series. Breath of the Wild on Switch 1 was my first Zelda experience, and I can't wait to finally play Ocarina of Time.
I've seen a few reports indicating that Amazon is suddenly delaying Ocarina of Time pre-orders by nearly a week.
To put it mildly, people are not happy .
Did you pre-order through Amazon? Are you seeing delays on delivery? Let me know in the comments or send me an email.
Our link to the Zelda console is broken and no longer goes to a page for the special edition Switch 2.
I tried searching for the console on the Walmart and nothing shows up. I tried links on other sites which now redirect to the Ocarina of Time remake.
I'll keep an eye on things but for now Walmart has vanished the 40th anniversary console and pro controller from its website.
The console have been sold out for a minute with no real restock coming in.
I decided to check out the Pro controllers just in case any of those were available instead.
Unfortunately, I'm not seeing it available anywhere. But I'll keep looking in case it pops up.
Did you know there are two cover variants of the Ocarina of Time physical edition?
There's a textured foil version and a normal. You'll know which you have if the spine lettering is gold (foil) or white (normal).
As of this posting here is what different retailers are offering. Foil cover:
The main UK retailers have been out of stock for most of the day, but I checked again just in case anyone is trying to get one before dinner.
Of the retailers I checked, Argos might have some but you'll need to put in your postal code to check. I tried several London codes and Bradford just to see but all those locations were out of stock.
We mentioned it above but as a reminder, if Target is your preferred or closest retailer, the company does not have stock today.
However, Target previously confirmed that it will open up sales on Friday (November 6).
That being said, I found claims on Reddit that some stores were selling the consoles today. It seems like those sold out quickly though.
Nintendo is selling an official playable Ocarina from the Ocarina of Time remake for $34.99. From my understanding it actually works.
Unfortunately, it's already sold out, but I'll keep an eye on things in case it pops back up.
Stock is not lasting long. I just posted about the official Nintendo Store twenty minutes ago and the Zelda console is already sold out.
With that in mind, lets take a look at all the retailers right now.
It should be noted that GameStop is in-store only. I checked in my area and was told that no store within 100 miles had stock. You might get luckier.
Also, Walmart features third-party sellers so you might see some availability but they're also gouging the price all the way up to $700. I recommend you avoid those.
If you prefer to get your gear directly from the source, it appears that the 40th Anniversary Switch 2 is available on the official Nintendo Store.
Check out the Nintendo Switch 2 - The Legend of Zelda - 40th Anniversary Edition for $519.99 on the Nintendo store.
Hopefully you managed to secure a Zelda Pro controller if that was on your wishlist during the Walmart restock. On my end the retailer is now once again showing the dreaded "sold out" message. I'm already watching for more restocks!
Last week, Target confirmed it would restock the Zelda Switch 2 console on Friday, November 6 via an update on its listing page, before removing said update, leading to fears the restock had been delayed. Good news! The message has returned, Target will restock tomorrow (Nov. 6) , and on the same day it will also restock the console in-store. So you can try both at your nearest Target and online.
It's not the console, but you can pick up the Zelda-themed Switch 2 Pro Controller at Walmart. The page already has a "low stock" warning though, so don't expect it to stick around long. If you want this nifty Switch 2 accessory, go grab it now.
If you're in the U.K. and haven't picked up your copy of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time yet, you can currently grab it for £54 on Amazon . That's a £5 saving. Not a huge discount, but any form of deal on a new release is pretty rare!
Sadly, on Amazon US, the game is listed at its standard $69 MSRP . In fact, it appears Ocarina is so popular that Amazon is having stock issues, with new orders not expected to arrive until November 12-13. So you might want to get it digitally.
Still nothing new to report on the restock front, so to pass the time, let me know your favorite The Legend of Zelda game in the above poll! I'd personally pick Breath of the Wild, but there are several classic Zelda games I still need to play.
With the U.S. starting to wake up, it's worth noting that the best chance of securing a Zelda Switch 2 today appears to be in-store rather than online. We know that Target, Best Buy, Walmart and GameStop have had in-store restock, though social media suggests the majority of inventory was snapped up during various midnight launch events. However, if you live local to a retailer, and don't mind taking the chance, you'll want to head over in person and try your luck!
It's Ocarina of Time launch day. The game is in the wild, and players are taking their first steps into this visually-stunning remake. If you haven't picked up your copy yet, what are you waiting for? I'll be diving into my own just arrived copy soon, but fear not, I'm still here for several more hours tracking Switch 2 restock!

The U.S. Army wants first dibs on American-produced heavy rare earths, and REalloys ( NASDAQ: ALOY ) has just signed a landmark nonbinding term sheet that could put it at the top of the military's supply chain list.
And the terms are extraordinary. The term sheet proposes a potential 75-year operating lease on approximately 200 acres at Tooele Army Depot in Utah, where REalloys would build and operate a facility processing dysprosium and terbium, two metals China has spent decades monopolizing .
In return, one of the things that the Army wants is the right of first offer on production, giving it an opportunity to secure the materials for American weapons manufacturers before they are offered to other buyers, although it is not obligated to purchase any.
This is the latest development in a relationship that began taking shape in June, when the Army selected REalloys for exclusive negotiations .
Now, the two sides have signed a term sheet spelling out the proposed commercial terms: an initial 50-year lease, a possible 25-year extension, government ownership of the land and a privately financed industrial operation that could help supply the military for generations. The term sheet is non-binding, and the final lease still requires financing and regulatory approvals.
Consider what the Army is proposing here.
Rather than waiting for a domestic rare earth industry to develop on its own, it is making military land available to a private producer and negotiating priority access to the output. The company would carry the cost of construction and operations, while the Army would gain a source of American-processed heavy rare earths, particularly dysprosium and terbium, which at or near the top of Washington’s metals wishlist.
Dysprosium and terbium are used in the high-performance magnets that keep working when temperatures climb inside fighter aircraft, missile systems, and advanced electric motors. Radar, sonar and precision-guided munitions also depend on specialized magnetic materials. The problem is that China controls almost all global processing of dysprosium and terbium, leaving American defense manufacturers exposed to Chinese export licensing decisions.
That dependence became painfully obvious when Beijing introduced export restrictions on seven categories of medium and heavy rare earths in April 2025 . Manufacturers suddenly faced delays, licensing requirements, and uncertainty over materials that had previously moved through established supply chains.
For the Pentagon, the stakes are unusually high.
Retired four-star General Jack Keane, who serves on REalloys' board, put the military consequences plainly in the company's announcement:. "For too long, the United States has depended on adversaries and others for the materials inside its most advanced defense technology and China has made clear it is prepared to use that dependence as leverage. Dysprosium and terbium sit at the center of that vulnerability. Our ability to deter conflict, and to prevail if deterrence fails, depends on producing munitions and weapons systems at scale, and that requires supply chains we control. This term sheet is an important step toward bringing heavy rare earth processing onto a U.S. defense installation. "
The Army's own Dr. Jeff Waksman was equally direct, describing rare earth processing as a national security vulnerability and pointing to China's near-total control of dysprosium and terbium.
The Pentagon has also imposed a deadline. Beginning January 1, 2027, expanded federal sourcing restrictions will apply to covered rare earth magnets and their supply chains. Defense contractors will need compliant sources of materials, processing, and manufacturing.
That creates an opening for companies capable of producing qualified rare earth metals outside China.
REalloys ( NASDAQ: ALOY ) has spent the past two years doing precisely that, securing feedstock, processing capacity, metallization technology, and financing across North America.
The company is already developing rare earth materials in Euclid, Ohio, and has partnered with Canada's Saskatchewan Research Council to expand non-Chinese rare earth processing.
Under that arrangement, REalloys secured rights to approximately 80% of SRC's expanded output, with the upgraded facility targeting annual production capacity of roughly 525 tonnes of NdPr metal, 30 tonnes of dysprosium oxide and 15 tonnes of terbium oxide
Those numbers are important because the rare earth business has a serious problem between the mine and the finished magnet.
Mining rare earths is one thing. Separating them, converting the oxides into metals and producing the alloys used in advanced magnets requires specialized equipment and technical expertise. China dominates those industrial processes, which is why simply opening new Western mines won't eliminate dependence on Chinese suppliers.
REalloys is developing what it says will become the largest heavy rare earth metallization facility outside China , with commissioning currently targeted for the first quarter of 2028.
The company has also secured a 15-year offtake agreement covering 15% of Phase 1 production from Critical Metals' Tanbreez project in Greenland, adding another potential source of rare earth feedstock outside China.
Other non-binding agreements involving Montana, Wyoming, and international partners expand the company's access to raw materials, while its strategic  LOI with JS Link aims to connect rare earth alloy production with permanent magnet manufacturing.
There's also a direct Pentagon relationship beyond Tooele.
In March, the Defense Logistics Agency awarded REalloys a contract to develop modular metallization technology for samarium and gadolinium, two additional metals used in specialized defense applications.
And the company has raised significant money to pursue its plans. REalloys completed an approximately $100 million institutional private placement in June and reported $122.4 million in cash at the end of that month.
Its Saskatchewan expansion and heavy rare earth metallization projects are funded through their planned commissioning stages, according to the company. Tooele remains a separate proposed development requiring its own financing and approvals.
The Army's approach at Tooele deserves attention because it could change how Washington develops domestic sources of critical materials.
Under the proposed arrangement, the government keeps the land. REalloys pays fair-market rent, finances construction, and runs the processing operation. Once production begins, the Army receives a contractual opportunity to buy the materials it needs.
The military would also receive participation rent once commercial operations begin, with the exact methodology to be negotiated in the definitive lease.
That means the Army could help establish domestic production on its own property while leaving construction and operating costs with the private sector.
And this is no ordinary short-term industrial lease.
The proposed initial term is 50 years, with a possible 25-year extension. That's a potential three-quarters of a century for a facility dedicated to materials that American defense manufacturers currently struggle to source outside China.
The proposed right of first offer is equally important. It would give the Army an opportunity to secure production from the facility, although it would not require the military to purchase any material.

articles.title_orig: Wendy's rejects buyout bid and girds itself for a hostile takeover campaign - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Wendy's rejects buyout bid and girds itself for a hostile takeover campaign - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Wendy’s rejected a $1.4 billion buyout offer from an activist investor, saying Thursday that the bid was too low
Wendy’s rejected a $1.4 billion buyout offer from an activist investor, saying Thursday that the bid was too low and didn't take into account the company's long-term earnings potential under its new CEO.
The Dublin, Ohio-based burger chain also said Thursday that its board had adopted a “poison pill” plan designed to make it more difficult to engineer a hostile takeover of the company.
Noted investor Nelson Peltz made an offer last week to buy the chain, which has been struggling with high beef prices and aging stores. Peltz said the fast-food landscape had become increasingly challenging, with consumers under pressure, intensifying competition and persistent inflation, and his offer was the best path forward for shareholders.
But in a conference call with investors Thursday, Wendy's CEO Bob Wright, who joined the company in May, said Wendy's has a turnaround plan in place that is already producing good results. Wright, who is the fourth CEO to lead Wendy's since 2024, was previously the president and CEO of Potbelly. He has also held senior leadership roles at Wendy's, Checkers and Domino's Pizza.
“We’re confident that we have the right strategy, execution and resources to restore Wendy’s to its full potential and drive meaningful shareholder value,” Wright said.
Shares rose less than 1% Thursday as the company reported a better than expected performance in the third quarter.
Wendy's said in a statement that a committee of independent directors unanimously rejected the offer because it “substantially undervalues” the company.
Wendy's shareholder rights plan — commonly known as a “poison pill" plan — grants all shareholders except a hostile bidder the right to purchase discounted shares and dilute the hostile bidder's ownership stake. It is automatically triggered if a person or group owns 15% or more of Wendy's shares.
Peltz's Trian Fund Management and other partners in the investor group that made the offer to Wendy's hold 16.3% of the company's shares. The plan would stay in place for one year, Wendy's said.
Trian didn't immediately respond to a request for comment Thursday. Peltz served as chairman of Wendy's board for 17 years until 2024. His son Bradley Peltz still serves on the company's board and is a Wendy's franchisee.
Dine Brands, the parent company of Applebee's and IHOP, adopted a similar one-year poison pill plan last week to fend off a takeover bid by two investment firms.
Founded in 1969 by Dave Thomas and named after his daughter, Wendy’s is known for its square burgers and Frosty desserts. The fast-growing chain introduced the drive-thru window in 1970 and went public in 1976. In the 1980s, as it jockeyed for sales with McDonald’s and Burger King, Wendy’s launched salad bars and ran its iconic “Where’s the beef?” ad campaign.
But as the fast-food market grew even more competitive and rival burger-focused chains like In-N-Out and Five Guys expanded, Wendy’s fell behind. Wendy’s share of U.S. burger chain sales fell from 11.5% in 2019 to 10.4% last year, according to Technomic, a market research company.
The industry has also been seeing lower U.S. traffic, especially from lower-income customers, as high gas prices and affordability concerns eat into household budgets. Third-quarter foot traffic fell 2.6% across the entire fast food sector in the U.S., according to Revenue Management Solutions, a restaurant industry consultant.
Wendy’s has been closing outdated U.S. restaurants so it can focus on its more profitable locations. The company closed 240 restaurants in 2024 and said earlier this year that it planned to shutter up to 358 locations in 2026.
Then, in September, one of the largest U.S. franchisees for Wendy’s filed for bankruptcy protection after the chain tried to terminate its franchise agreement. Michigan-based Meritage Hospitality Group operates 314 Wendy’s restaurants in 15 states.
Under Wright, Wendy's has launched a turnaround plan dubbed Dave's Way, which calls for improving food quality, more distinctive marketing and improved digital ordering and restaurant operations.
Wright said Thursday that Wendy's has begun testing quality improvements, including thicker and crispier bacon, creamier Frosties and whole-leaf lettuce on sandwiches. The company is removing lower-volume items from its menus to reduce complexity in its kitchens and making breakfast optional, allowing franchisees to focus on their most profitable times of day.
Wendy's on Thursday reported revenue of $547 million in the July-September period. That was better than the $531 million Wall Street had forecast, according to analysts polled by FactSet. Wendy's same-store sales, or sales at locations open at least a year, fell 5.2%, which was also better than the 6.4% drop analysts forecast.
Wendy’s had 5,969 restaurants in the U.S. and 1,428 outlets in 38 countries at the end of 2025.

articles.title_orig: 'Too early' to say if Europe flight bomb threats linked, EU says
articles.title_zh: 'Too early' to say if Europe flight bomb threats linked, EU says
articles.content_orig:
The EU said on Thursday it was not yet clear whether a spate of hoax bomb alerts targeting European flights were connected and that it was following events closely with national authorities.
"Any threats against civilians are unacceptable," EU transport commissioner Apostolos Tzitzikostas posted on X, adding that it was "too early to draw conclusions on whether the reported incidents are linked."
The statement from Brussels comes after Italian, French and Bulgarian fighter jets scrambled as at least 27 European flights were hit by hoax bomb alerts for the third day this week, authorities and airlines said.
The hoaxes particularly targeted low-cost carriers and flights to or from Bulgaria, Czech Republic and Italy.
Italian air force jets escorted a Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome while French fighters guided a Aer Lingus Dublin-Rome flight to a military base outside Paris. Bulgaria's air force escorted three planes targeted by threats.
Three flights were diverted in all but all the jets landed safely with no explosives found.
More than 20 hoaxes have now been reported this week with low-cost carrier Ryanair the victim of at least seven.
Three Ryanair planes headed for Sofia from Madrid, Copenhagen, and London Stansted were targeted by bomb threats, a spokesperson for the Bulgarian Ministry of Transport said.
Two of the planes landed in Sofia but the flight from London-Stansted was diverted to Plovdiv Airport, east of the capital.
Air force fighter jets escorted all three planes, the defence ministry said, saying such missions "detect, identify and escort the aircraft."
All three planes were later inspected, and no explosives were found, an interior ministry spokesperson told the AFP news agency.
A Finnair flight from Helsinki to Rome was escorted to Rome by a fighter jet and checked by bomb experts, a Rome Fiumicino Airport spokesperson told AFP.
A Finnair spokesperson Stiina Tuunanen, confirmed that "nothing unusual was found" when the jet landed.
Finnair has a “very clear process that we follow in situations like this and we always work closely with the local authorities," Tuunanen said.
She said another false bomb threat had targeted flight AY1471 from Helsinki to Vienna, without providing further information.
After receiving a threat, a Wizz Air flight from Milan to Warsaw was re-routed to Vienna, the airline said, "in accordance with established safety protocols and procedures".
Another Wizz Air flight from Milan to Bucharest landed at its destination safely, "following which a crisis unit was set up at Henri Coanda Airport," the Romanian intelligence service said in a statement.
An Aer Lingus flight from Dublin to Rome was rerouted to France after a bomb threat. It was escorted by military aircraft to the Evreux air base west of Paris, French authorities said.
"The flight landed safely and Aer Lingus will work to reaccommodate customers to their final destination as soon as possible,” the airline said in a statement.
Four Prague-bound planes flown by Ryanair, Easy Jet and Sky Express were also the target of threats.
"We perceive the credibility of the threats as low," said Czech police on X. "Nevertheless, we are not underestimating the situation and all necessary security measures have been activated."
Prague Airport spokeswoman Denisa Hejtmankova told AFP the airport had received all the threats in emails from anonymous addresses. It was not immediately clear which airlines were involved.
Two planes, meanwhile, that arrived at Copenhagen were also the object of threats.
"Our assessment is that there is no danger, and there has never been any danger, to passengers or anyone else at the airport," Copenhagen police told AFP.
The origin and motives of the threats were unknown, but come amid a rise in hybrid attacks in Europe, sometimes linked by authorities to Russia or Iran.
France's secretary general for defence and national security, Nicolas Roche, highlighted to parliament last month "the massing of hybrid attacks in all their diversity — sabotage, cyber, drones, espionage of course —that we are seeing take shape in Europe."
On Tuesday, 27 flights were targeted with bomb threats, all of which turned out to be hoaxes.
The alerts forced the closure of a Warsaw airport and the deployment of Italian air force jets to protect flights.
On Monday, a Wizz Air flight from London's Luton airport to Sofia was diverted due to a bomb threat and forced to make an emergency stop in Budapest.

articles.title_orig: After 3 Months Lost at Sea, Five Survivors Are Rescued on Remote Island
articles.title_zh: After 3 Months Lost at Sea, Five Survivors Are Rescued on Remote Island
articles.content_orig:
Five people, including two children, were rescued this week in the South Pacific island nation of Kiribati after three months drifting at sea in a 20-foot skiff, authorities said. Another four remained missing.
Villagers rescued the group Sunday off Fanning Island in Kiribati, the Australian Broadcasting Corp. reported , after they had drifted an estimated 3,355 miles east from the Federated States of Micronesia.
The U.S. Coast Guard in Guam on Tuesday confirmed that the skiff with nine people aboard had been reported missing after it failed to return to Ruo Island in Micronesia on July 30. The group had been making a one-hour crossing between the islands of Murilo and Ruo at the time, ABC reported.
A 10-day search covering 33,000 square miles followed without any sign of the missing boat or those aboard, it said.
"Incredible and wonderful news these five folks were found and are receiving care," the U.S. Coast Guard told The Associated Press in an email.
"Our profound condolences to family and friends of those who did not arrive with them," the email added.
When asked by the AP what happened to the missing four, the U.S. Coast Guard said it was continuing to gather and confirm information and would reply as soon as possible.
A lawmaker in Kiribati, Kaotitaake Rakoroa, told ABC the survivors were being cared for by a pastor on the island.
Nursing officer Paukin Tororo told the ABC on Monday that all five were severely dehydrated and malnourished. They were put on intravenous drips and were showing signs of recovery.
"They can give a smile face, they show the sign they want to eat," she told the ABC.
The survivors had yet to speak publicly about their ordeal and had requested privacy, the Australian broadcaster reported. ABC said the group went missing after their boat was caught in a storm.
The governor of Micronesia's Chuuk state, Alexander Narruhn, issued a statement Sunday saying he had begun talks with the Kiribati government to bring the survivors home.
"There were nine people aboard the boat that went missing. Thanks be to God for his love and mercy that five of the nine have been found," Narruhn said through an interpreter.
"We continue to pray for their four companions," he added. Narruhn did not immediately respond to the AP's request for comment.
There have been previous incidents where people have become lost at sea among the tiny island chains that stud the Pacific Ocean. An Australian man survived more than two months lost at sea in 2023 with his dog Bella after rough seas damaged their boat and its electronics system. Tim Shaddock, 51, had been traveling from Mexico to French Polynesia, but found himself drifting in the Pacific Ocean for more than two months. Shaddock and his canine companion survived by drinking rain water and eating raw fish that Shaddock caught, he said. They were spotted by a helicopter and rescued in July 2023.
Two American sailors and their two dogs were rescued after five months at sea in the Pacific in 2017. Jennifer Appel and Tasha Fuiaba were discovered 900 miles southeast of Japan by a Taiwanese fishing ship, the U.S. Navy said at the time. The vessel's engine died during bad weather, and they were unable to get to land using the ship's sails. The women said the boat drifted off course, and no ships were near enough to hear their distress calls. Water purifiers and a year's supply of food aboard the vessel kept them alive, the Navy said.
In 2024, three fishermen were stranded on a remote Micronesian island for more than a week . They were rescued after using palm leaves to spell out "HELP" in large letters on a beach.

articles.title_orig: Top Democrats call to rein in AI buildout after midterms sweep: 'National data center moratorium now'
articles.title_zh: Top Democrats call to rein in AI buildout after midterms sweep: 'National data center moratorium now'
articles.content_orig:
After a big win in the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, some Democrats are already signaling they want to take on the artificial build-out, specifically data centers.
In a post on X , Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., touted referendums across the U.S. on Tuesday where voters in localities approved restrictions on data centers . Sanders, who caucuses with the Democrats, said the message to political leaders is clear.
"National data center moratorium now," he wrote in the post. "Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future."
In another post on X, Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., wrote that pausing AI development needs to be a top priority for the large Democratic majority in the House on Day 1. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, amplified the post and said, "Yes!"
According to the CNBC Voter Poll , 56% of voters said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision at the ballot box. Of those voters, 65% said they cast a ballot for a Democratic candidate for Congress.
Stocks linked to the artificial intelligence build-out declined slightly on Wednesday in the wake of the election, but the selling intensified on Thursday as investors worried Democratic wins could have a real impact on data center construction. Chip stocks led the decline. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) tumbled nearly 9% on Tuesday. Nvidia declined 8%, while Advanced Micro Devices sunk more than 14%.
Democrats who flipped critical races on Tuesday also singled out big tech companies and data centers.
South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews, who flipped a Senate seat in the state on Tuesday, launched a website during the campaign that branded her opponent — Sen. Darline Graham — "data center Darline."
In her victory speech on Tuesday, Andrews said voters chose a South Carolina "where decisions about communities are made by the people who live in our communities, not the billionaires or data center companies in Washington D.C."
Ohio Democrat Sherrod Brown , who is heading back to the Senate after defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Jon Husted on Tuesday, said in his victory speech, "I do not work for data centers."
Democratic governors also attacked data centers in their victory speeches. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who signed an executive order in August to slow data center development, said big tech companies shouldn't determine residents' futures. "Instead, the folks in our local communities get the final say," he said.
Perhaps most important to the data center build-out is Texas, which is home to 27% of planned data center capacity, according to Wells Fargo.
Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who ousted incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, didn't address data centers directly in her victory speech, though they played a key role in her campaign.
"When I am governor, I will issue a moratorium, a ban, on all data center approvals until laws can be passed by the legislature to protect Texans," she said in a video posted to her X in late October. "This is about one fight. Is this going to be a Texas that is by and for the people, or is this the billionaire's world and we just live here? Data centers are part of that fight."

articles.content_orig:
Russian President Vladimir Putin received Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, in Moscow Thursday to discuss strengthening ties between their two countries, including a pipeline to import Russian gas.
Speaking to journalists after their meeting, Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, called it "an extremely important exchange," according to remarks reported by the Iranian embassy.
"During the meeting with Mr. Vladimir Putin, discussions were held regarding the construction of gas pipelines from Russia to Iran," said Rezaei, Iranian state TV reported.
He noted the aim was to enable Iran "to address its own gas shortages while also facilitating the sale of Russian gas to neighbouring countries."
While a major producer, Iran has long suffered shortages of natural gas, essential for powering heating systems, which have been exacerbated by the war with the United States and Israel.
During the most intense phase of the fighting, which lasted nearly 40 days, the U.S. and Israel struck key Iranian infrastructure including natural gas refineries, according to Tehran.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi spent much of the day on calls with his counterparts from several Middle Eastern countries, including Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Turkey.
In total, Araghchi held calls with nine different countries in the Middle East. Few details were shared about what was discussed on the calls, simply nodding to "diplomatic efforts to maintain stability in the region."
Notably, Pakistan was one of those countries involved as they have been very closely involved as mediators in U.S.-Iran peace talks. Araghchi spoke to their foreign minister, Ishaq Dar, on Thursday evening.
Araghchi also spoke to Saudi foreign ministers Faisal bin Farhan and Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman, despite accusations of Iranian involvement in attacks on that country by the Houthi militia in Yemen.
President Trump's administration held secret talks with Iran on deporting Iranians even as the war there dragged on, court documents obtained by The Associated Press show.
The court documents unsealed Thursday show the Republican administration as recently as mid-October said it had plans to deport the Iranians through an unnamed third country, although it was unclear when it intended to do so. The judge in the case ordered the government to give the court 24-hour notice of any finalized plans to deport Iranians to Iran or to any other country and five days' written notice before any such deportation is carried out.
The documents show the administration maintained contacts with Iranian officials during the war over the removals, specifically for submitting travel documents and figuring out "possible avenues for removal."
"We are at war with a country where the President of the United States has said, as recently as two or three days ago, if not yesterday, that it is essentially lawless ... A country that is an enemy of the United States, according to the current president. A country that, according to our president, murdered tens of thousands of protestors," Judge Ana Reyes said according to the Oct. 15 transcript.
"And what you're telling me is that the United States of America is going to send individuals back to that region, facing what you and I and everyone who would ever look at this would know would be, at a minimum, a serious threat of certain death."
"Yes, your honor," Justice Department attorney Dimitar Georgiev-Remmel said. "The government is executing lawful orders of removal."
The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The Houthis took credit for disrupting travel using a drone at King Fahd International Airport on Thursday.
"We targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam using a drone and our operation caused a disruption of air navigation at the airport," Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree said on X.
The city of Dammam, which is located in the oil-rich eastern part of Saudi Arabia, and King Fahd airport have been regular targets for Houthi attacks. Multiple drones have disrupted traffic at the airport this week, according to past announcements.
Two people were killed in a Houthi strike on King Fahd airport on Oct. 22.
The USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and its associated strike group will make a port call in Singapore Friday and will not reach the Middle East for at least another two weeks, a U.S. official told CBS News on Thursday.
There are already two carrier strike groups in the region and, which officials say is sufficient firepower to execute any commands issued by President Trump.
Mr. Trump has not signaled yet, in the wake of the U.S. midterm elections, whether he intends to order major new strikes on Iran — an option he kept on the table with repeated statements ahead of Tuesday's voting.
The initial knee-jerk reaction to the U.S. midterm election results faded a bit Thursday.
The price of a barrel of Brent crude oil, considered the international standard, rose 2.2% to $96.70, recovering a chunk of its nearly 9% drop from the day before.
Uncertainty still reigns about what will happen in the war with Iran and when the global energy industry can return to normal.
Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, met Thursday in Moscow with Russian President Vladimir Putin to deliver a message from Iran's supreme leader, according to the Iranian government.
They met amid uncertainty over President Trump's next move on Iran in the wake of U.S. midterm election results that represented a major rebuke of his policies, including, he has admitted, the decision to launch the war with Iran alongside Israel more than eight months ago.
Mr. Trump said repeatedly ahead of the Tuesday vote that he had yet to make a decision on whether to order major new attacks on Iran or to agree a deal to end the war, which Tehran has so far refused to do until the U.S. accepts its core demands to end its naval blockade, ensure a halt to fighting on all fronts in the Middle East, and ease sanctions.
During the Rezaei-Putin meeting in Moscow on Thursday, the Russian Foreign Ministry warned Russian citizens against all travel to Iran.
"Given the continued risk of a new escalation around Iran, our recommendations to Russian citizens remain unchanged," ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told reporters in Moscow. "We recommend temporarily refraining from traveling to that country until the situation is resolved. We also ask our compatriots already in Iran to exercise vigilance and avoid crowds, public events, and areas near military and government facilities."
She said the guidance was "based on the official information disseminated by Tehran," without providing any further detail.
The Iranian Foreign Ministry renewed the regime's rejection on Thursday of longtime and widely held beliefs that Tehran materially supports the Houthi rebels fighting the Saudi Arabia-backed government in Yemen's decade-long civil war. The conflict intensified a couple months ago and quickly became the most active and deadly front in the intertwined conflicts in the Middle East.
Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei called the latest accusation of Iranian support for the Houthis, made Monday by European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, "baseless," and said Iran "strongly denied claims that Iranian military experts were present in Yemen."
The U.S. government, along with many other Western nations and the NATO alliance , have demanded for years that Iran stop supporting the Houthis. The support, according to these nations, includes financial backing, weapons and other equipment, and direct coordination and training.

Reports said the attacks struck Russiaâs third-largest oil refinery and a Wildberries logistics hub in the western Ryazan region, setting both ablaze.
Wildberries processes almost a million orders a day and has been described as a Russian version of Amazon.
âFires broke out at industrial facilities in Ryazan. Power lines were damaged, causing electricity disruptions in parts of the city,â regional Governor Pavel Malkov said .
Ukraine has spent months pummeling Russiaâs oil refineries with drone strikes.

Malkov said one person was injured in the strikes, and falling drone debris also caused damage.

articles.title_orig: Nier: Automata’s latest update increases game size from 50GB to 366GB
articles.title_zh: Nier: Automata’s latest update increases game size from 50GB to 366GB
articles.content_orig:
An update has ballooned Nier: Automata’s file size to 366GB on Steam.
This is seemingly caused by a bug that has added the full game’s file size to the file size of each DLC. When stacked up, it means you will need 366GB of space to install the full game and its adds-ons, despite it only being around 50GB prior to the update being pushed out.
While initially suspected to be a typo on Steam , RPG Site has since tested this out and indeed found that Nier: Automata now requires 366GB of space. It’s likely the bug will be addressed in a hotfix soon, so it’s worth holding off on installing Nier: Automata or the new update until then. It’s also a handy reminder to switch off auto updates on Steam if you’re unable to revert back right now.
Some report that the issue is fixed on their end, but others are still showing inflated file sizes when they go to install the game or the new update. The store page still says that you just need 50GB of space to install the game. It only seems that you’ll be asked for the additional space when you actually attempt to install it after purchase.
Curiously, the update that caused this hasn’t even added much to the game, instead adding support for three new languages (Korean, Simplified Chinese, and Traditional Chinese).
Unsurprisingly, the game is seeing some negative reviews come in, seemingly from those unable to play the game now that it wants to eat up so much space on their PCs. Right now, neither Square Enix nor Platinum Games has acknowledged the mistake, so it’s unclear when a fix will be rolled out everywhere.

iPhone Duo has only been available for a couple weeks, but Apple keeps improving the product with software enhancements. The latest arrives in the iOS 27.3 beta via a convenient keyboard update.

iPhone Duo shipped with iOS 27.1, but just a few days later iOS 27.2 arrived and added Apple Pencil support and Edge Light for video calls.

Reachability lets you slide outer display content to the left or right to make it more reachable. And as highlighted by Beta Profiles on X , the keyboard has gotten an improvement too.
iOS 27.3 beta tweaks iPhone Duo's outer display keyboard, with narrower keys and a slightly thinner, smaller font. pic.twitter.com/BDKCBZc52Z
The keyboard refresh with narrower keys and smaller font makes it easier than before to type on the iPhone Duo’s outer screen, especially one-handed.
It’s a subtle difference, but one that early testers have found a clear upgrade.
By combining keyboard changes with Reachability, iOS 27.3 offers a noteworthy improvement to the one-handed iPhone Duo experience.

articles.content_orig:

Muse Voice, a feature that lets users call and video chat with Meta’s consumer AI agent, Muse, is now available to everyone in the U.S., the company announced on Thursday.
First introduced at Meta’s Connect developer conference in September, the video-chatting feature involves new AI models, Muse Realtime Avatar and Muse Realtime Voice technology, which help power the digital avatar that chats with the user.
While other AI competitors offer voice chat features, Meta’s Muse offers a cute, animated avatar (nicknamed Jolly), which users interact with as they ask questions or request tasks to be handled on their behalf. Users can also customize the avatar as they choose, changing it to something that looks more like a person, animal, or some other character.
The company believes that anthropomorphizing Muse in this way could make consumers feel more connected to their AI agent — a connection that could grow even stronger as they begin to engage in live conversations with it.
As the Muse avatar speaks, Meta says it will use “subtle expressions and gestures” that match the tone of the conversation. (Muse doesn’t actually “see” the user, but it hears them and reacts based on their conversations.)
The news of the rollout was announced via blog post and on X by Meta’s chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang, who shared a demo of his Muse in action. The video saw Wang joking around, referencing his love of posting memes on X, which he told his Muse may have gotten him in trouble with his boss. His Muse, a fluffy white dog, responds with a suggestion to add disclaimers to those memes that could be misinterpreted as Meta endorsing anything risqué. (Ha!)
The added support for video chats and calls comes just before Meta’s plan to launch a Tamagotchi-like wearable device for its Muse AI agent before year-end. When the device arrives, the digital avatar will appear on its small screen, letting users talk to the agent, which can then reply or carry out tasks for them.
Meta says the real-time conversations are supported on mobile, web, and Mac and will later come to its AI Glasses and the upcoming “Muse Charm” hardware device.

articles.title_orig: A Phenomenon: Initial Applications for Unemployment Benefits (4-Week Average) Drop to the Lowest since 1969
articles.title_zh: A Phenomenon: Initial Applications for Unemployment Benefits (4-Week Average) Drop to the Lowest since 1969
articles.content_orig:
The four-week average of initial applications for unemployment insurance benefits fell to 194,700, the lowest since 1969, according to the Labor Department today. For just the week through Saturday, initial applications for unemployment benefits fell to 189,000, same as in mid-July, and both were the lowest since 1969.
But the population, the labor force, and employment are vastly bigger now than in the 1960s. So these initial applications, historically low in absolute terms, are amazingly low in relative terms.
The four-week average irons out the week-to-week volatility caused by some states missing the reporting deadline, with those weekly claims then falling into the following week. The purple columns indicate recessions, and what happens to initial claims for unemployment benefits before and during recessions.
There have been waves of layoffs at some companies through the left door, while they hired through the right door – big tech has been doing that now since 2022. Overall, private-sector companies have added to their payrolls at a lethargic pace, with some sectors experiencing labor shortages and hiring booms, and other sectors (such as mortgage lending in 2022 and 2023 and some corners of tech) having experienced substantial payroll reductions. Where Are the Jobs? Winners and Losers by Industry .
In addition, the federal government has shed 328,000 workers since January 2025, and state governments (mostly higher education) have shed 53,000 workers since January 2025.
Laid-off staff who receive severance packages, such as continued salaries for x number of months, cannot file for unemployment benefits since they’re still getting paid by their former employer. Many of them find new jobs within the severance period, collect severance plus the salary at the new job, and so they cannot claim unemployment benefits and don’t show up on the unemployment rolls.
But people who could not find a new job within the severance period are eligible to file for unemployment benefits when the severance expires. Their initial applications for unemployment benefits show up here in the data.
Laid-off H-1B visa holders are generally not eligible to file for unemployment insurance benefits and don’t show up in the data here.
What we’re seeing here is that the crackdown on illegal immigration and on abuses of legal immigration rules has changed the labor market by reducing the supply of labor over the past 18 months, and confirms what the separate data in the monthly employment report has also shown from a different angle.
This declining labor force has kept the labor market relatively tight.
Normally , that combination of big job losses at the federal and state governments, and lethargic payroll increases in the private sector, amid a normally growing labor force, would have led to surging claims for unemployment insurance, and by extension surging unemployment rates (data in the jobs report, the next one tomorrow).
The fact that this hasn’t happened shows the impact of the crackdown on illegal immigration which has caused the labor force to decline this year.
Continued weekly claims for unemployment insurance benefits reflect the total number of people who’d initially applied for unemployment insurance at least a week earlier and who still haven’t found a job and are still claiming unemployment benefits.
Continued claims ticked up to 1.72 million in the latest reporting week, with the four-week average at 1.71 million. The only periods since the 1960s when continued claims were lower were some weeks in 2018-2019 and during the labor shortages after Covid.
With initial claims being very low — meaning, the influx into continued claims is very low — rising or falling continued claims suggest the direction of how long it takes overall for laid-off people to get a new job after claiming unemployment insurance.
When it takes longer overall for them to find a new job and they spend more time on the unemployment insurance rolls, these continued claims rise, and they did that coming out of the labor shortages – but remained historically low.
For the past 12 months, the trend has turned the other way, with people spending less time unemployed before they find a new job, and the number of continued claims has declined since late 2025.

articles.title_orig: Kimberly-Clark beat earnings estimates as China furor weighs on sales
articles.title_zh: Kimberly-Clark beat earnings estimates as China furor weighs on sales
articles.content_orig:
Organic sales fell 1.3%, including a 270 basis point headwind from the China social media disruption; the company kept its 2026 outlook
SOPA Images / Getty Images
Kimberly-Clark $KMB reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $1.70 a share from continuing operations on Thursday, up 17.2% from a year earlier, as a social media disruption in China weighed on sales.
Adjusted earnings topped the $1.65 a share that analysts expected, according to The Wall Street Journal . Net sales fell 0.4% to $4.1 billion, and organic sales declined 1.3%, including a headwind of about 270 basis points from the China disruption, the company said.
Adjusted earnings per share attributable to Kimberly-Clark , which include discontinued operations, fell 6.6% to $1.70. Diluted earnings per share attributable to the company were $5.37, compared with $1.34 a year earlier. The latest quarter included a pre-tax gain of about $1.4 billion from the completion of its International Family Care and Professional business transaction with Suzano, which closed July 1.
In International Personal Care, organic sales fell 4.6%, including a headwind of about 770 basis points from China. Segment operating profit fell 32.7% to $144 million. North America organic sales rose 0.4%.
Adjusted operating profit was $677 million, down 0.9%, with the China disruption accounting for a headwind of about 530 basis points. Adjusted gross margin was 35.5%, down 130 basis points from a year earlier.
"Our third quarter results reflect a dynamic operating environment and several discrete impacts," Chairman and CEO Mike Hsu said in a statement.
In October, Chinese authorities said a multi-agency investigation found no formamide in the diapers it tested, including Kimberly-Clark ’s, and no health hazards from the claimed chemical, according to Reuters.
The company kept its 2026 outlook. It expects organic sales growth about 100 basis points below the 1.7% weighted average growth of its categories and countries, reflecting about 100 basis points of impact from the China disruptions. It expects adjusted operating profit to grow in the mid-single digits on a constant-currency basis. It expects adjusted earnings per share from continuing operations to grow in the high single digits, and adjusted earnings per share attributable to Kimberly-Clark to decline in the low single digits, both on a constant-currency basis.
Kimberly-Clark acquired Kenvue, the maker of Tylenol, on Nov. 2. In October, the company had weighed a bond offering to help finance the Kenvue takeover , a deal valued at roughly $36 billion that included $6.7 billion in cash. JPMorgan $JPM Chase had supplied $7.7 billion of bridge financing for the transaction.

articles.title_orig: The ‘Musk selloff’ deepens as Tesla and SpaceX combine for $450 billion two-day wipeout
articles.title_zh: The ‘Musk selloff’ deepens as Tesla and SpaceX combine for $450 billion two-day wipeout
articles.content_orig:
The two companies helmed by the world's richest person have had a rough two-day stretch on the market. Tesla ( TSLA -10.77% ) closed at $398.50 on Election Day, and by 3:08 p.m. ET Thursday, it was trading at about $342, down 14%, representing a loss of about $225 billion in market value. SpaceX ( SPCX -9.05% ) fell from $141.31 to about $125, down 12%, or about $227 billion. Together, that's about $450 billion gone in two sessions, most of it on Thursday, when Tesla fell about 11% and SpaceX about 8%.
To illustrate how steep the drop has been, SpaceX is now trading below its $135 IPO price from June.
Image source: Getty Images.
If you had to sum it up in one word: politics. Democrats now control both chambers of Congress, and Musk, a top ally of President Donald Trump, is a likely target. Speaking on the All-In podcast on election night, Texas Republican Sen. Ted Cruz said Democrats had signaled they would use subpoenas "to go after Elon Musk." In Texas, home to both companies, voters elected a Democratic attorney general for the first time since 1994.
But political sentiment isn't the only reason. The Nasdaq was headed for its worst day in 18 months on Thursday as investors dumped chip and data-center stocks, on fears that new leaders in Washington and the states could slow data-center construction. SpaceX, of course, is exposed: Last month, it committed to a roughly $40 billion lease for AI chips with an entity managed by Apollo Global Management, with payments starting in the first half of 2027.
Adding to the fire for SpaceX, Wall Street is reportedly trying to sell off pieces of that $40 billion chip deal to other investors, with Goldman Sachs and Apollo leading the effort, according to Bloomberg on Thursday.
SpaceX made money last quarter: $2.79 billion in operating income and $4.4 billion in net income, though it's still $413 million in the red for the first nine months of the year. Nothing that happened in Washington this week changes its launch business or Starlink.
But the fine print, or at least the filing details, are worth noting. That net income included a $390 million tax benefit and a $561 million unrealized gain on its stake in the Boring Company, Musk's tunneling firm, and two customers made up about half of quarterly revenue. Even after the drop, SpaceX is valued at about $1.7 trillion, roughly 150 times its third-quarter operating income on an annualized basis.
Part of Tesla's bull case rests on robotaxis. On Tesla's October earnings call , CFO Vaibhav Taneja told analysts he expects robotaxis to make a real dent in both sales and profits in 2027, and the firm said the Cybercab was due to launch in Dallas this month. Musk told analysts Tesla will end up doing "a majority of all passenger miles on earth" -- "unless we are stopped by governments."
That caveat matters more this week. Self-driving cars depend on regulators, and Washington just got less friendly to Musk. Taneja also conceded that the robotaxi business hasn't yet reached its cost target of 30 cents per mile.
The two companies are also tied together. Tesla's filing puts its SpaceX stake at $2.87 billion as of Sept. 30, and shows SpaceX with a $729 million balance owed to Tesla, most of it tied to Megapack batteries still on order. Bad news for one tends to hit the other.
Not all at once. The political risk is real, but for now it's mostly talk. The new Congress isn't seated until January, and investigations take time. Meanwhile, a two-day drop of 12% to 14% doesn't make either stock cheap.
If you believe in Musk's long-term plans, this is a reasonable time to start a position slowly. Buy in small pieces over several weeks, and keep it a small part of your portfolio, because these are among the most volatile tech stocks you can own.
If you can only pick one, SpaceX gives you a launch and satellite business that's already earning money, while much of Tesla's value rides on robotaxis that are just getting started. And if headlines out of Washington would keep you up at night, it's fine to wait until the political picture is clearer.

articles.title_orig: Goldman Sachs buries DEI metrics as it names biggest partner class since 2010
articles.title_zh: Goldman Sachs buries DEI metrics as it names biggest partner class since 2010
articles.content_orig:
Goldman Sachs is burying the diversity metrics of its newest partner class — blaming a changed legal environment as it swells its elite ranks to a 16-year high to fight off defections.
The Wall Street giant led by CEO David Solomon tapped 109 employees on Thursday to join its partnership on Jan. 1, marking the largest promotion cycle since 2010.
As many as 30% of the new class hails from the asset and wealth management division, signaling Goldman’s pivot toward steady fees. A record 13 engineers made partner as the financial giant integrates artificial intelligence across the trading floors.
But in a stark departure from recent years, Goldman refused to provide a racial or gender breakdown of the newly minted rainmakers.
During a background briefing with reporters, executives dodged questions about the missing demographic data, citing the changed legal environment across corporate America.
The comments appeared to be a thinly-veiled reference to the Trump administration’s drive to stamp out so-called Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion policies nationwide.
Internally, bosses have said aiming to build a diverse workforce makes Goldman a better company.
In its previous class announced two years ago, Goldman named 95 new partners. Among them, 27% were women, 6% were Hispanic or Latino and 4% were Black.
The public pivot abruptly ends Goldman’s long-running DEI victory laps and exposes Wall Street’s growing fear of reverse-discrimination lawsuits following the Supreme Court’s crackdown on affirmative action.
While guarding the exact makeup of the 2026 class, the bank disclosed one metric, noting it will cross a milestone of more than 100 female partners out of a total pool of just over 500. Goldman currently employs more than 47,000 worldwide.
Asked by The Post if the supersized class was a desperate maneuver to prevent top earners from jumping to private equity rivals like Apollo and Blackstone, a Goldman executive insisted the partnership hasn’t “lost its luster.”
The bank pointed out that firm revenues have jumped roughly 60% since 2018, keeping the overall percentage of partners at roughly 1% of the workforce.
John Waldron, the chief operating officer and president, was in talks in 2024 to join Marc Rowan’s Apollo, but stayed at 200 West Street after being handed a $80 million stock retention bonus by the board in January 2025.
Waldron is seen as the heir apparent when Solomon finally calls it a day as CEO.
The firm’s newly minted rainmakers can nab yearly salaries north of $1 million, but the staggering wealth of the partnership lies in its secretive, closely guarded bonus pools.
Making the cut grants immediate entry into exclusive, performance-based year-end payout structures that routinely double or triple a partner’s base pay in a good market.
The partner title also unlocks access to Goldman’s proprietary internal investment vehicles, allowing them to personally co-invest their wealth alongside the firm in highly lucrative private equity funds while dodging steep client fees.
Goldman noted 39% of the new class joined as campus hires and 28% started as summer interns.
The incoming partners average 17 years at the bank and hold 20 different citizenships . Sixty-two are based in the Americas, 27 in EMEA, and 20 in the Asia Pacific region .
